lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Did you know Moirichus the rich man, Diogenes? The very rich one, from Corinth—the man with all the cargo-ships? His nephew was Aristeas, also rich. He used to quote that line from Homer: “Either lift me up, or I lift you.”

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: They were courting each other for the inheritance. Same age, both of them. Each had put his will on public display: Moirichus naming Aristeas master of everything, if Moirichus died first; Aristeas naming Moirichus, if he got out ahead of him. That was all in writing. Meanwhile they were outdoing one another in flattery. The prophets were no help—the astrologers, the dream-readers, the whole Chaldaean nursery, and even Apollo at Delphi himself: one moment the prize was Aristeas’s, the next it was Moirichus’s. The talents kept tipping—now to that side, now to this one.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And how did it end, Crates? This sounds worth hearing.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: They both died on the same day. Both inheritances went to Eunomius and Thrasycles—relatives, both of them, and neither of them had ever been tipped by a prophet that things would turn out this way. Moirichus and Aristeas were sailing from Sicyon to Cirrha; halfway across, they caught the Iapyx on the beam and capsized.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Good. When we were alive, we never had thoughts like that about each other. I never once prayed for Antisthenes to die so I could inherit his staff—though it was a very sturdy one, made of wild olive. And I don’t suppose you, Crates, were longing to inherit my estate when I died: the jar, the wallet, and the two quarts of lupins in it.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: I had no need of any of that. Nor did you, Diogenes. What mattered, you inherited from Antisthenes, and I from you—possessions far greater and more dignified than the empire of Persia.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Wisdom. Self-sufficiency. Truth. Plain speech. Freedom.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: By Zeus, yes. I remember inheriting that fortune from Antisthenes—and leaving you an even larger one.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: But everyone else ignored that sort of property. Nobody courted us in expectation of inheriting it. They all had their eyes on the gold.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Naturally. They had nowhere to receive such things from us. Luxury had made them leaky, like rotten money-bags. So if anyone did drop wisdom into them, or plain speech, or truth, it fell straight out and drained away; the bottom couldn’t hold it. Like those daughters of Danaus, forever pouring water into the perforated jar. Gold, though—that they guarded with teeth and nails and every device available.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: So we shall keep our wealth even here. The others arrive carrying one obol—and even that only as far as the ferryman.
